chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Talhah ibn Zayd, from Ja'far, from his father (peace be upon them both).

That a man freed part of his slave boy and said, 'He is completely free, not for God to have a partner.' He said, 'I see that upon him is fifty lashes and he seeks forgiveness from God.' I said, 'What do you think if she made him free and forgave him?' He said, 'No beating upon him if she forgave him before she raises (her case to the judge).' I said, 'And does she cover her head from him when she freed half of her?' He said, 'Yes, and she prays while her head is covered and she does not marry until she pays what is upon her or the other half is freed.'

Because in this report it is not that the female slave was entirely his, but it is not impossible that the meaning is when he did not own from her except half of her. And if he owned all of her, she would have been freed according to what the first two reports contained. And upon this interpretation, there is no contradiction between the reports.

key_terms.نِصْفُ الْكِنْيَةِ: Half-owned slave (specifically female concubine context here)

ai.seo_question: What are the legal consequences and conditions when a master frees only part of his slave?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq clarifies the fiqh of partial manumission (itq al-nisf), establishing that the slave remains in a state of 'mudabbar' status until the remaining share is freed or the master dies. It highlights the practical legal implications for the slave woman, such as her eligibility to pray and marry while still partially owned, provided she covers her head, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the gradual liberation process. The text concludes by reconciling apparent contradictions in other narrations by specifying that the rulings apply specifically to cases of partial ownership rather than total manumission.
